title: W3C DTCG Format — The Universal Token Standard
content: The W3C Design Token Community Group (DTCG) format is the emerging universal standard for design tokens, enabling interoperability between Figma, Token Studio, Style Dictionary, and code. Each token is a JSON object with a $value and $type field. Token types: color, dimension, fontFamily, fontWeight, fontSize, lineHeight, letterSpacing, duration, cubicBezier, number, boolean. Example: { "color-primary-500": { "$value": "oklch(0.55 0.18 250)", "$type": "color" } }. Group tokens with nesting: { "color": { "primary": { "500": { "$value": "...", "$type": "color" } } } }. Alias syntax uses curly braces: { "$value": "{color.primary.500}" }. TOOLS: Token Studio for Figma reads and writes DTCG format and syncs with GitHub/GitLab. Style Dictionary transforms DTCG tokens to platform outputs (CSS variables, iOS Swift, Android XML). Theo by Salesforce is another transformer. WHY IT MATTERS: a DTCG-compliant token file is tool-agnostic — you can switch between design tools and code pipelines without reformatting. Define tokens once, use everywhere.

title: Neutral Colour Naming — Fills, Strokes, Alt Model
content: An alternative to generic shade-number naming (gray-100 through gray-900) is naming neutrals by their application role. Three categories: FILLS — the lightest shades used as backgrounds and surface fills. Fill-1 (lightest, page background), Fill-2 (card background), Fill-3 (elevated surface). STROKES — medium-intensity values for borders and dividers. Stroke-1 (subtle divider), Stroke-2 (default border), Stroke-3 (strong border). ALT — semi-transparent colours for overlays, hover states, and tinted highlights. Alt-1 (hover tint, ~5% opacity), Alt-2 (pressed tint, ~10% opacity), Alt-3 (selection highlight, ~15% opacity). This approach aligns naming to designer intent rather than raw lightness values — a designer always knows whether they need a fill, a stroke, or an overlay, even without knowing the exact shade number. DARK MODE: Fills invert (dark background becomes Fill-1), Strokes remap to lighter values, Alt opacity values stay the same but the base colour changes. Combine with numeric intensity suffixes where needed: Fill-1, Fill-2, Fill-3. This naming model works alongside semantic tokens — Fills/Strokes/Alt are primitives that semantic tokens reference.

title: State Naming Conventions — Interactive States
content: Interactive component states require consistent naming across all tokens. Standard state vocabulary: DEFAULT (or no suffix) — resting state, no interaction. HOVER — cursor over element (web only). PRESSED — mouse/touch down. ACTIVE — currently selected or toggled on (e.g., active tab). FOCUS — keyboard focus ring visible. DISABLED — non-interactive, reduced opacity or muted colour. VISITED — for links only. LOADING — async operation in progress. ERROR — validation failure. SUCCESS — operation completed. Token naming with states: color/action/primary/default, color/action/primary/hover, color/action/primary/pressed, color/action/primary/disabled. RULE: Never abbreviate states (no 'hvr' or 'dis'). RULE: Default state tokens may omit the '/default' suffix in short names (color/action/primary) but should be explicit in verbose naming. RULE: Disabled states typically reference the same hue but at reduced opacity (40-50%) or a muted neutral — never a completely different colour.

title: Token Scale Conventions — Numeric vs T-Shirt vs Named
content: Three conventions for expressing scale, each with trade-offs. NUMERIC (100-900 or 50-950): Most common for colour primitives. Conveys relative intensity — 100 is light, 900 is dark. Easy to extend (add 25, 125 etc). Framing: higher number = darker (Tailwind, Material). Downside: changing a value breaks the semantic meaning of the number (if you darken 500, is it still 500?). T-SHIRT (xs, sm, md, lg, xl, 2xl, 3xl): Best for spacing, border-radius, font-size. Communicates relative size, not absolute value. Survives value changes — md stays md even if the px value shifts. 7–9 steps covers most needs. NAMED (subtle, default, strong): Best for semantic tokens where the relationship matters more than the position. text/secondary/default, border/default, surface/strong. Communicates hierarchy and usage intent. RECOMMENDATION: colour primitives → numeric 50-950. Spacing, radius, font-size → t-shirt. Semantic tokens → named. Never mix conventions within the same layer — all primitives use one system, all semantics use another.

title: Component Token Naming Patterns
content: Component tokens follow the pattern: [component]-[slot]-[property]-[variant]-[state]. Component: the UI component name (button, input, card, badge). Slot: the sub-element within the component (label, icon, border, bg, shadow). Property: the CSS property being controlled (color, bg, radius, padding-x, padding-y, height, gap). Variant: the component variant (primary, secondary, ghost, danger). State: the interactive state (default, hover, focus, disabled). Examples: button-bg-primary-default → maps to action-primary-default. button-bg-primary-hover → maps to action-primary-hover. input-border-focus → maps to action-primary-default. input-bg-disabled → maps to surface-muted. card-radius → maps to radius/lg. badge-bg-success → maps to success-subtle (a semantic token). RULE: Component tokens only ever reference semantic tokens, never primitives. RULE: Not every property needs a component token — create component tokens only when the value might need to be overridden independently of the semantic layer (e.g., a ghost button that needs its own hover background that's different from the semantic hover colour).

title: Variable Collection and Mode Naming
content: Collection naming should reflect the token layer and domain: PRIMITIVES collection (or split: Primitives/Colour, Primitives/Spacing) — one mode (values don't change). SEMANTICS collection — modes: Light (default), Dark. SPACING collection — modes: Comfortable (default), Compact. TYPOGRAPHY collection — modes: Desktop (default), Mobile. BRAND collection — modes: Brand-A (default), Brand-B, Brand-C. Mode naming conventions: capitalize first word, keep short (Light/Dark not LightMode/DarkMode). Default mode is always listed first — it applies when no mode is explicitly set. COLLECTION NAMING RULES: avoid generic names (no 'Tokens' or 'Variables'). Name by what the collection controls: 'Colour/Semantics', 'Spacing', 'Typography'. PREFIX CONVENTION: prefix primitives with a symbol or emoji to separate them visually in the panel (e.g. '● Primitives', '◆ Semantics') — this is optional but helps in large files. RULE: All variables in a collection share the same modes. If some colour variables need Light/Dark and others need Brand modes, they belong in separate collections.

title: Boolean Variable Naming Patterns
content: Boolean variables control layer visibility and feature flags. Naming convention: use affirmative names (not negative). GOOD: show-icon, has-avatar, is-active, feature-flag/show-banner. BAD: hide-icon, no-avatar, not-active. Affirmative naming means true=visible/active and false=hidden/inactive — consistent with CSS display logic. PATTERNS: show-[element]: show-icon, show-badge, show-description, show-label. has-[element]: has-image, has-avatar, has-footer. is-[state]: is-loading, is-active (though state is usually handled by variants, not booleans). feature-flag/[name]: feature-flag/dark-mode, feature-flag/new-checkout — for product feature toggling via modes. SCOPING: Boolean variables should be scoped to 'Show/hide layer' only. They should not appear in colour or spacing dropdowns. MODES: boolean variables can have modes — show-feature-banner might be true in Brand-A mode and false in Brand-B. This enables mode-driven feature toggling without creating separate component variants.

title: Grid and Layout Token Naming
content: Layout tokens define the structural grid of the interface. COLUMN COUNT: grid/columns/mobile=4, grid/columns/tablet=8, grid/columns/desktop=12. These are number variables. GUTTER (gap between columns): grid/gutter/mobile=16px, grid/gutter/tablet=24px, grid/gutter/desktop=24px. MARGIN (edge padding): grid/margin/mobile=16px, grid/margin/tablet=32px, grid/margin/desktop=64px. CONTAINER MAX-WIDTH: layout/container/sm=640px, layout/container/md=768px, layout/container/lg=1024px, layout/container/xl=1280px, layout/container/2xl=1536px. BREAKPOINTS: breakpoint/sm=640, breakpoint/md=768, breakpoint/lg=1024, breakpoint/xl=1280, breakpoint/2xl=1536. Breakpoints are number variables documenting values in px without the unit. RESPONSIVE MODE APPROACH: instead of separate breakpoint variables, create a Layout collection with modes: Mobile/Tablet/Desktop. Each mode carries the appropriate column count, gutter, and margin values. Switching the frame mode updates all layout references instantly. FIGMA GRID STYLES: create Figma grid styles named Grid/Mobile-4col, Grid/Tablet-8col, Grid/Desktop-12col and reference the variable values. This links the visual grid overlay to the token values.

title: Slash Hierarchy Depth and Grouping Strategy
content: Slash notation in Figma variable and style names creates visual grouping. DEPTH: aim for 2-3 levels. Two levels for simple systems (color/primary-500), three for complex (color/action/primary/hover). Four or more levels become hard to navigate — flatten where possible. GROUPING STRATEGY: Group by domain first, not by type. DO: color/text/primary, color/text/secondary, color/surface/default. DON'T: text/color/primary, surface/color/default (type before domain makes the panel hierarchy confusing). ALIGNMENT WITH CODE: slash hierarchy maps to CSS custom property naming (--color-text-primary) and DTCG JSON nesting ({ color: { text: { primary: {} } } }). Design and code token names should be identical or differ only in separator (slash vs hyphen). RULES: Be consistent — never mix slash and camelCase within the same collection. Capitalize mode names (Light, Dark, Desktop, Mobile) but use lowercase for token names. Use plural for group names only when the group contains multiple items of that type — 'colors' is wrong for a group of one colour, 'text' is correct for a group of text colour tokens. NUMBER OF TOP-LEVEL GROUPS: 5-8 is manageable. More than 10 top-level groups signals the collection should be split.
